title: Thread-safe notification dispatch
idea: A thread-safe notification service changes shared state, like the key map and counters, atomically, and calls slow providers with no lock held.

analogy.text: A mailroom with four clerks and one sign-out sheet. The first clerk to sign for a parcel delivers it; others see the signature and move on.
analogy.breaks: Two clerks can both see a blank line; `putIfAbsent` cannot.

points: Two workers can receive the same request when a caller or queue retries.
Get-then-put on the key map lets both workers send the same SMS.
`putIfAbsent` makes claiming a key one atomic step: one winner sends.
A bounded queue with `CallerRunsPolicy` slows producers instead of exhausting memory.

steps.caption: Unsafe version. W-1 asks the map whether `k1` was seen.
Before W-1 writes, W-2 asks the same question.
Both workers hold the answer no.
W-1 claims `k1` and sends the OTP.
W-2 acts on its stale no. The user gets the same OTP twice.
Safe version. Both workers call `putIfAbsent` at once.
The map applies one call first. W-1 finds no owner and writes itself.
W-2 gets W-1 back as the owner, so it drops the request.
Only the winner calls the provider, outside any lock. One OTP is sent.

code.title: Prove the duplicate
code.caption: A barrier makes both workers look before either writes, so the duplicate shows up on every run.

walk.text: Run the same race twice: get-then-put first, then `putIfAbsent`.
A thread-safe map, a two-party barrier, and a counter of SMS sends.
Safe: `putIfAbsent` returns null only to the one call that wrote.
Unsafe: each call is thread-safe, but the pair is not. Both send.
Join both threads before reading the count, so output is stable.

code.title: Worker pool
code.caption: Four workers process 200 requests with 50 duplicates, while the primary provider fails every third call.

walk.text: sms-a fails every third call; sms-b never fails.
Four threads and a queue of 20. When it is full, the submitting thread runs the task.
Wait for every task to finish before printing.
Shared state: an immutable provider list, a concurrent map and atomic counters.
Ids come from an `AtomicLong`; the key claim is one atomic call.
The winner fails over across providers with no lock held during the slow call.

pitfalls: Never send inside `computeIfAbsent`; it holds a bin lock and can block other updates.
Do not share a plain `int` id counter across threads; use an `AtomicLong`.
Use a bounded queue; an unbounded one hides overload until memory runs out.

quiz.q: What does Dispatcher print for sms-b?
options: It changes from run to run
quiz.why: Only 150 keys win the claim, so sms-a gets 150 calls and fails every third: 50. Each failure fails over to sms-b once.

takeaway: Claim the key atomically, then send with no lock held.

starters: Why is ConcurrentHashMap alone not enough to stop duplicate sends?
What happens to claimed keys if the worker crashes before sending?
How do I keep one user's notifications in order across worker threads?
